part_title: EBS Performance Bottlenecks, Snapshot Consistency and Restore Readiness

scenes.title: Find the narrowest point in the EBS path
scenes.visual_overview: The approved slide teaches find the narrowest point in the ebs path through a service architecture and explanation panels.
visual_walkthrough: Follow application I/O sizes and queue depth to the EBS request path
Compare the volume's configured IOPS, throughput and latency to the actual workload
Inspect the EC2 instance EBS bandwidth or IOPS ceiling before adjusting only the volume
scenes.visual_example: An instance can cap throughput even after the volume has been provisioned for more bandwidth; the bottleneck must be measured across both layers.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Performance tuning must target the actual constrained part of the path.
scenes.narration: This slide walks through the EBS performance path from the application to the volume. Start with I/O size and queue depth. An application making small random requests produces a different operations-per-second and throughput relationship from a sequential data scan that uses large blocks. Next, inspect the provisioned volume limits: IOPS, throughput, latency and queueing should be considered together. Then follow the connection back to the EC2 instance. The instance has its own EBS bandwidth and IOPS ceilings, so paying for a larger volume configuration cannot overcome a smaller instance-side limit. For example, a database administrator might increase provisioned IOPS and observe no improvement because the EC2 instance is already saturating its EBS path. The correct response is to measure CloudWatch and application metrics, identify the limiting layer, and adjust either instance choice, volume parameters or application I/O behavior accordingly. The slowest link defines the effective performance.

scenes.title: Snapshots capture changed blocks, not application intent
scenes.visual_overview: The approved slide teaches snapshots capture changed blocks, not application intent through a service architecture and explanation panels.
visual_walkthrough: Trace incremental block changes across the first and subsequent EBS snapshots
Differentiate snapshot storage from customer-managed S3 object storage
Explain application-consistent snapshots, coordinated multi-volume capture and testing restores
scenes.visual_example: A database backup procedure quiesces writes and coordinates relevant data and log volumes, rather than assuming a crash-consistent block image meets recovery requirements.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Incremental storage efficiency does not guarantee an application-consistent recovery point.
scenes.narration: This slide explains what an EBS snapshot protects and what it does not. The first snapshot represents the used blocks of a volume, and later snapshots store changed blocks incrementally. Removing an earlier snapshot does not automatically invalidate a newer snapshot because the snapshot service manages the necessary block references. The next station distinguishes snapshot storage from ordinary objects in your own S3 buckets. EBS snapshots are managed recovery resources backed by S3 infrastructure, not customer-accessible snapshot object files. The final station is the most important operational check: a block-level capture does not automatically preserve application intent. For databases or multiple linked volumes, coordinate writes and use an application-consistent procedure where required. A database may need its data and logs captured in a compatible state, not just a volume image from an arbitrary moment. A reliable design pairs snapshot policy with real restore exercises and documented consistency requirements.

scenes.title: Restore in the target AZ and plan first-read latency
scenes.visual_overview: The approved slide teaches restore in the target az and plan first-read latency through a service architecture and explanation panels.
visual_walkthrough: Explain the EBS snapshot-to-new-volume restore path within the target Availability Zone
Show why restored data can exhibit first-read initialization effects
Compare prewarming, Fast Snapshot Restore and supported provisioned-rate initialization choices
scenes.visual_example: A recovered analytics instance starts slowly on its first data scan because restored blocks are being initialized; a tested restore plan can account for this.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Restored volume creation is not equal to application readiness.
scenes.narration: This diagram follows recovery from an EBS snapshot into a new volume. First select the destination Availability Zone and create the volume there, then attach it to a compatible EC2 instance and complete any required operating-system setup. The middle panel shows an important performance caveat. A restored volume can experience additional latency while blocks are initialized on first access, so a successful Create Volume operation is not the same as meeting the application's recovery-time objective. The last panel compares ways to manage that effect. Depending on requirements, teams may read blocks in advance, use Fast Snapshot Restore, or consider supported provisioned-rate initialization options, each with specific costs and constraints. Imagine a large analytics workload recovering after a zone failure. The instance may boot while the first working-set scan remains slow. The architecture must measure time until useful application performance, not merely the instant when a volume reaches the available state.
